lehigh-2022-01.title: Evaluate at 1
lehigh-2022-01.body:
The sum of the coefficients of $p$ is $p(1)=(1-1-1)^{2022}=(-1)^{2022}=1$.

**Answer: 1**

lehigh-2022-02.title: Count squares
lehigh-2022-02.body:
Among the integers $1,\dots,N$ there are $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ squares, so $N-\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ non-squares. For $N=1032$: $\lfloor\sqrt{1032}\rfloor=32$ (as $32^2=1024<1032<33^2=1089$), so there are $1032-32=1000$ non-squares up to $1032$, and $1032$ is not a square itself. Hence $a_{1000}=1032$.

**Answer: 1032**

lehigh-2022-03.title: Solve the equation
lehigh-2022-03.body:
$f(f(x))=\dfrac1{1+\frac2{1+2x}}=\dfrac{1+2x}{3+2x}$. Setting this equal to $x$: $1+2x=3x+2x^2$, so $2x^2+x-1=0$, with roots $x=-1$ and $x=\frac12$ (both satisfy $f(x)=x$, and neither makes a denominator zero). Their sum is $-\frac12$.

**Answer: $-\frac12$**

lehigh-2022-04.title: Divisor-count shapes
lehigh-2022-04.body:
For $p>3$, $p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)$ is divisible by $2$ and by $3$ ($p=2,3$ give $3$ and $8$, with $2$ and $4$ divisors). A number with exactly $10$ divisors has the form $q^9$ or $q^4r$ with distinct primes; being divisible by both $2$ and $3$ forces $q^4r\in\{2^4\cdot3,\,3^4\cdot2\}=\{48,162\}$. Then $p^2=49$ or $163$; only $49$ is a square, so $p=7$ ($48=7^2-1$ has divisors $(4+1)(1+1)=10$).

**Answer: 7**

lehigh-2022-05.title: Complete a fourth power
lehigh-2022-05.body:
Adding $x^2$ to both sides: $x^4-4x^3+6x^2-4x+1=x^2$, i.e. $(x-1)^4=x^2$, so $(x-1)^2=\pm x$. The case $(x-1)^2=-x$, i.e. $x^2-x+1=0$, has no real roots. The case $(x-1)^2=x$, i.e. $x^2-3x+1=0$, has roots $\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}2$ with sum $S=3$ and product $P=1$. So $\lfloor S+P\rfloor=4$.

**Answer: 4**

lehigh-2022-06.title: Square of centers
lehigh-2022-06.body:
The centers of the four unit circles form a square of side $2$ with diagonal $2\sqrt2$. A circle tangent to all four and inside (in the middle) is centered at the center of the square, at distance $\sqrt2$ from each unit center, so its radius is $r=\sqrt2-1$. A circle tangent to all four on the outside (enclosing them) has radius $R$ with $R-1=\sqrt2$, so $R=\sqrt2+1$. The ratio is $\frac{\sqrt2+1}{\sqrt2-1}=(\sqrt2+1)^2=3+2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $3+2\sqrt2$**

lehigh-2022-07.title: Mod 9, then check
lehigh-2022-07.body:
A number and its digit sum are congruent mod $9$. With $k=2$ we need $2x\equiv x\pmod9$, so $9\mid x$: $x\in\{18,27,36,45,54,63,72,81,90,99\}$. Now check each. Failures: $27\cdot7=189$, $36\cdot8=288$, $54\cdot7=378$, $63\cdot3=189$, $72\cdot4=288$, $81\cdot6=486$ each have digit sum $18$ instead of $9$. The remaining four work: the multiples $18k$ ($36,54,72,90,108,126,144,162,180$) and $45k$ ($90,135,180,225,270,315,360,405,450$) and $90k$ all have digit sum $9$, and the multiples $99k$ ($198,297,\dots,990$) all have digit sum $18=$ the digit sum of $99$. So $x\in\{18,45,90,99\}$ and the sum is $252$.

**Answer: 252**

lehigh-2022-09.title: Fixed point of the tower
lehigh-2022-09.body:
The sequence $a_n=X^{a_{n-1}}$ converges (since $X<e^{1/e}$) to the attracting fixed point $Y$ of $Y=X^Y$, equivalently $X=Y^{1/Y}$. Since $X=\left(\frac{10}9\right)^{1/(10/9)}$, $Y=\frac{10}9$ satisfies this, and it is attracting: the derivative of $t\mapsto X^t$ at $Y$ is $X^Y\ln X=Y\ln X=\ln\frac{10}9\approx0.105<1$. The convergence is geometric with ratio $\approx0.105$, so $a_{1000}$ equals $\frac{10}9$ to many more digits than needed. Then $1000a_{1000}\approx1111.11$, and the closest integer is $1111$.

**Answer: 1111**

lehigh-2022-10.title: Pairs of steps
lehigh-2022-10.body:
The graph is $A-B-C$, $C-D-E$, $C-F-G$. The vertices $B,D,F$ each have exactly $2$ neighbours, and every neighbour of $B,D,F$ is one of $A,C,E,G$ (and vice versa), so a path alternates between these two groups. From any of $B,D,F$, two steps lead to $4$ different endings: for $B$, they are $B\to A\to B$, $B\to C\to B$, $B\to C\to D$, $B\to C\to F$, ending again in $\{B,D,F\}$; the same count holds from $D$ and $F$. So a path of length $4$ from $B$ has $4\cdot4=16$ possibilities, and from the endpoint (one of $B,D,F$) the fifth step has $2$ choices: $16\cdot2=32$.

**Answer: 32**

lehigh-2022-10.title: Direct count by steps
lehigh-2022-10.body:
Count the paths ending at each vertex after $n$ steps. $n=1$: $A:1$, $C:1$. $n=2$: $B:2$, $D:1$, $F:1$. $n=3$: $A:2$, $C:4$, $E:1$, $G:1$. $n=4$: $B:6$, $D:5$, $F:5$ (total $16$). $n=5$: each of the $16$ paths ends at $B$, $D$ or $F$ with $2$ continuations: $32$.

**Answer: 32**

lehigh-2022-11.title: Angle at B
lehigh-2022-11.body:
Triangle $ABE$ has sides $4,3,5$, so $\angle AEB=90^\circ$. Since $CD\parallel AB$ and $BF\perp CD$, also $BF\perp AB$. Therefore $\angle EBF=90^\circ-\angle ABE$, so $\cos\angle EBF=\sin\angle ABE=\frac45$ ($\sin\angle ABE=\frac{AE}{AB}$). By the law of cosines in $EBF$: $EF^2=BE^2+BF^2-2\cdot BE\cdot BF\cdot\frac45=9+25-24=10$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{10}$**

lehigh-2022-11.title: Coordinates
lehigh-2022-11.body:
Let $A=(0,0)$, $E=(4,0)$, $B=(4,3)$ (right angle at $E$) and $D=(d,0)$. The line $CD$ is parallel to $AB$ (direction $(4,3)$) through $D$ and at distance $5$ from $B$, which is at distance $d\cdot\frac35$ from line $AB$; so $d=\frac{25}3$. The foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $CD$ is $F=B+(3,-4)=(7,-1)$ (the other choice, $(1,7)$, is not on line $CD$). Then $EF=\sqrt{(7-4)^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{10}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{10}$**

lehigh-2022-12.title: Write Kim's apartment by floor
lehigh-2022-12.body:
Let Chris's apartment number be $C$; then Kim lives on floor $C$, so Kim's apartment is $10(C-1)+x$ with $1\le x\le10$. The sum is $10(C-1)+x+C=239$, so $11C=249-x$. The only multiple of $11$ among $239,\dots,248$ is $242$, so $x=7$ and $C=22$. Kim's apartment is $10\cdot21+7=217$ (Chris's is $22$; check $217+22=239$).

**Answer: 217**

lehigh-2022-14.title: Finite differences
lehigh-2022-14.body:
Successive differences: $8,26,72,188,440,918\to18,46,116,252,478\to28,70,136,226\to42,66,90\to24,24$. The fourth differences are constant ($24$), as expected for a quartic. Extend: fourth row $24,24,24$; third row $42,66,90,114$; second row $28,70,136,226,340$; first row $18,46,116,252,478,818$; values $\dots,918,1736$. So $p(7)=918+818=1736$.

**Answer: 1736**

lehigh-2022-15.title: Inclusion-exclusion
lehigh-2022-15.body:
Count seatings up to rotation: $5!=120$ equally likely. Gluing one couple into a block: $3\cdot(2\cdot4!)=144$ seatings; gluing two couples: $3\cdot(2^2\cdot3!)=72$; gluing all three: $2^3\cdot2!=16$. Seatings with no adjacent couple: $120-144+72-16=32$. Probability $\frac{32}{120}=\frac4{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac4{15}$**

lehigh-2022-15.title: Direct count
lehigh-2022-15.body:
Seat Mr. A at seat $0$ of seats $0,\dots,5$; the other $5$ people can be arranged in $120$ ways. If Mrs. A is opposite (seat $3$), the remaining seats are $1,2$ and $4,5$ and the only adjacent pairs among them are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{4,5\}$; these must not be couples, giving $4!-8=16$ arrangements. If Mrs. A is at seat $2$ (similarly seat $4$), the remaining seats $1,3,4,5$ have adjacent pairs $\{3,4\}$, $\{4,5\}$. The person in seat $4$ must have their spouse in seat $1$ (otherwise the spouse is adjacent), which gives $4$ choices for that person and then $2$ ways to place the other couple in seats $3,5$: $8$ arrangements per seat, $16$ in total. Mrs. A at seats $1$ or $5$ is adjacent to Mr. A and is excluded. Total $16+16=32$ out of $120$: $\frac4{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac4{15}$**

lehigh-2022-16.title: Total sum two ways
lehigh-2022-16.body:
Let $S$ be the sum of the first column; the column sums are $S,4S,16S$, so the total is $21S$. Let the row sums be $r,r+6,r+12$; the total is $3r+18$. So $21S=3r+18$, i.e. $7S=r+6$, so $r\equiv1\pmod7$. One row sum is $2022$, so $r\in\{2022,2016,2010\}$. Only $r=2010$ gives $r+6=2016$ divisible by $7$: $S=\frac{2016}7=288$.

**Answer: 288**

lehigh-2022-17.title: Reflections
lehigh-2022-17.body:
Let $P=(1,7)$. A shortest closed path visits a point $Q$ on the $y$-axis and a point $R$ on $y=x$: $P\to Q\to R\to P$ (the other order gives the same bound). Reflect $P$ across the $y$-axis to $P_1=(-1,7)$ and across $y=x$ to $P_2=(7,1)$. Then $PQ=P_1Q$ and $RP=RP_2$, so the length is $P_1Q+QR+RP_2\ge P_1P_2=\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=10$. Equality holds when $Q$ and $R$ lie on segment $P_1P_2$ in that order: it crosses the $y$-axis at $Q=(0,6.25)$ and then the line $y=x$ at $R=(\frac{25}7,\frac{25}7)$.

**Answer: 10**

lehigh-2022-18.title: Divisibility by 9 and 11
lehigh-2022-18.body:
Divisible by $9$: the digit sum is a multiple of $9$; all digits are even, so the digit sum is a multiple of $18$. Divisible by $11$: (sum of digits in odd positions) $-$ (sum in even positions) is a multiple of $11$, and being even it is a multiple of $22$. Let the position sums be $u$ and $v$ (both even). Then $u+v\in\{18,36,\dots\}$ and $u-v\in\{0,\pm22,\dots\}$. If $u+v=18$: $u=v=9$ is odd, and $|u-v|=22$ is impossible; so $u+v\ge36$ and $u=v=18$ (or $|u-v|\ge22$, which needs larger digit sums). With fewer than $6$ digits one of the two groups has at most $2$ digits (sum $\le16<18$), so we need at least $6$ digits. For six digits: positions $1,3,5$ sum to $18$ and positions $2,4,6$ sum to $18$. To minimize, take the first digit $2$ (it cannot be $0$), then the other two odd-position digits sum to $16$, so they are $8,8$. Even positions: smallest second digit $2$, then $8,8$. The number is $228888=99\cdot2312$.

**Answer: 228888**

lehigh-2022-20.title: Euclid's algorithm
lehigh-2022-20.body:
If $d$ divides both, it divides their difference $(n+1)^2+1-(n^2+1)=2n+1$. Then $d\mid(2n+1)^2-4(n^2+1)=4n-3$, and so $d\mid2(2n+1)-(4n-3)=5$. Thus $d\le5$, and $n=2$ gives $5$ and $10$, with common divisor $5$.

**Answer: 5**

lehigh-2022-21.title: Minimize |7p-5q|/(7q)
lehigh-2022-21.body:
$\left|\frac pq-\frac57\right|=\frac{|7p-5q|}{7q}$. For $q\ge8$ the fraction cannot equal $\frac57$ (a reduced fraction equal to $\frac57$ has $q=7$), so $|7p-5q|\ge1$. Solutions of $7p-5q=\pm1$ need $q\equiv3$ or $4\pmod7$; the largest such $q\le99$ are $94$ (giving $\frac{67}{94}$) and $95$ (giving $\frac{68}{95}$, as $7\cdot68-5\cdot95=1$). The distance for $q=95$ is $\frac1{665}$. Any fraction with $|7p-5q|=1$ and smaller $q$ is farther, and any fraction with $|7p-5q|\ge2$ is at distance at least $\frac2{7\cdot99}=\frac2{693}>\frac1{665}$. So $\frac{68}{95}$ is the closest ($\gcd(68,95)=1$).

**Answer: $\frac{68}{95}$**

lehigh-2022-22.title: Linearity of expectation
lehigh-2022-22.body:
For each possible block of three consecutive rolls, count the probability that it is a maximal run of exactly three $6$s. Blocks at an end of the sequence (positions $1$-$3$ and $8$-$10$) need the three rolls to be $6$ and the single neighbour not a $6$: $\left(\frac16\right)^3\cdot\frac56$ each. Blocks in the interior (starting at positions $2,\dots,7$: six of them) need both neighbours to be non-$6$: $\left(\frac16\right)^3\left(\frac56\right)^2$ each. Expected number $=2\cdot\frac1{216}\cdot\frac56+6\cdot\frac1{216}\cdot\frac{25}{36}=\frac1{216}\left(\frac{5}{3}+\frac{25}6\right)=\frac1{216}\cdot\frac{35}6=\frac{35}{1296}$.

**Answer: $\frac{35}{1296}$**

lehigh-2022-23.title: Orbit counting
lehigh-2022-23.body:
Without identifying rotations there are $6!=720$ colorings of the six faces. The rotation group of the cube has $24$ elements (choose which face goes to the top: $6$ ways, then $4$ rotations), and since all colors are distinct, no nontrivial rotation fixes a coloring, so each coloring has $24$ equivalent versions. The number of distinct colorings is $\frac{720}{24}=30$.

**Answer: 30**

lehigh-2022-24.title: Bound the sum of squares
lehigh-2022-24.body:
Center the cube at the origin; the three faces lie in the planes $x=1$, $y=1$, $z=1$. The points are $A=(1,\cos\alpha_1,\sin\alpha_1)$, $B=(\sin\alpha_2,1,\cos\alpha_2)$, $C=(\cos\alpha_3,\sin\alpha_3,1)$. Direct expansion gives $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2=18-2\sum_{i}(1+\sin\alpha_i)(1+\cos\alpha_{i+1})$ (indices mod $3$). Each term in the sum is $\ge0$, so $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2\le18$. By Cauchy-Schwarz, the perimeter is at most $\sqrt{3\cdot18}=3\sqrt6$. Equality: take $A=(1,0,-1)$, $B=(-1,1,0)$, $C=(0,-1,1)$: every term $(1+\sin\alpha_i)(1+\cos\alpha_{i+1})$ vanishes and each side has length $\sqrt6$, so the perimeter is $3\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt6$**

lehigh-2022-25.title: Extinction probability
lehigh-2022-25.body:
Let $q$ be the probability that the population starting from one organism eventually dies off. Then a population of $k$ organisms dies off with probability $q^k$, and conditioning on the first hour: $q=\frac14(1+q+q^2+q^3)$, i.e. $q^3+q^2-3q+1=0$, which factors as $(q-1)(q^2+2q-1)=0$. The extinction probability is the smallest root in $[0,1]$: $q=\sqrt2-1$ (the root $q=1$ is the trivial one). So $p=1-q=2-\sqrt2\approx0.5858$ and $100p\approx58.6$, closest integer $59$.

**Answer: 59**

lehigh-2022-26.title: Zigzag and cycles
lehigh-2022-26.body:
The path $R\,(LR)^{99}R^{100}$ (turns in order) achieves $100\sqrt2$: the first $200$ steps zigzag, each pair of steps advancing by $(1,1)$ in some direction, for a displacement of $100\sqrt2$, and the final $100$ right turns make $25$ complete unit squares, which return to the same point. For the upper bound, a path whose first turn is $L$ decomposes as $L(R^{k_1}L)\cdots(R^{k_{98}}L)R^{k_{99}}$; each block between consecutive left turns, $R^{k}L$, has displacement of length at most $\sqrt2$, and there are at most $100$ such blocks, so the total displacement is at most $100\sqrt2$ by the triangle inequality. A path starting with $R$ is bounded in the same way using blocks $R^{k_1}\,(LR^{k_2})\cdots(LR^{k_{100}})$. (As a check we verified the analogous formula $(L+1)\sqrt2$ by exhaustive computer search for smaller turn counts with $R-L-1\equiv0\pmod 4$.)

**Answer: $100\sqrt2$**

lehigh-2022-27.title: Orthocenter
lehigh-2022-27.body:
Let $H$ be the orthocenter, the intersection of $AD$ and $BE$. Since $\angle CDH=\angle CEH=90^\circ$, the points $D,E$ lie on the circle with diameter $CH$, so this is the circumcircle of $CDE$. We need $CH$. From the law of cosines, $169=196+225-2\cdot14\cdot15\cos C$, so $\cos C=\frac35$. In triangle $ACD$ (right at $D$) $CD=AC\cos C=9$, and $BD=14-9=5$, $AD=12$. In triangle $BDH$ (similar to $CDA$, since $\angle DBH=90^\circ-C=\angle DAC$), $DH=BD\cdot\frac{CD}{AD}=5\cdot\frac9{12}=\frac{15}4$. Then $CH=\sqrt{CD^2+DH^2}=\sqrt{81+\frac{225}{16}}=\frac{39}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{39}4$**

lehigh-2022-28.title: Compare consecutive n
lehigh-2022-28.body:
Work mod $13$. The value being constant means $a^{n+1}+b^{n+10}\equiv a^n+b^{n+9}$, i.e. $a^n(a-1)\equiv-b^{n+9}(b-1)$ for all $n\ge1$. If $a=1$ then $b^{n+9}(b-1)\equiv0$ forces $b=1$: the pair $(1,1)$ works. If $a\ne1$, the left side is nonzero, so $b\ne1$ and dividing the equations for $n+1$ and $n$ gives $a\equiv b$. Then $a^n(a-1)\equiv-a^{n+9}(a-1)$, so $a^9\equiv-1$. Then $a^{18}\equiv1$ and with $a^{12}\equiv1$ we get $a^6\equiv1$, hence $a^3\equiv a^9a^{-6}\equiv-1$. The cube roots of $-1$ mod $13$ are $12,4,10$ ($4^3=64\equiv-1$, $10^3=1000\equiv-1$). All three work. So $S=\{(1,1),(4,4),(10,10),(12,12)\}$ and the sum of first coordinates is $1+4+10+12=27$.

**Answer: 27**

lehigh-2022-29.title: Growth rate
lehigh-2022-29.body:
Let $r$ be the positive root of $P(x)=x^3-x^2-x-b$ (the characteristic polynomial). By induction there are positive constants $c_1,c_2$ with $c_1r^n\le a_n\le c_2r^n$. So $\sum\frac{a_n}{4^n}$ behaves like $\sum(r/4)^n$: it converges if $r<4$ and diverges if $r\ge4$. Since $P(x)\to\infty$ and $P$ has exactly one positive root, $r<4$ iff $P(4)>0$, i.e. $64-16-4-b>0$, $b<44$. For $b=44$, $P(4)=0$, so $r=4$ and the series diverges. The smallest such $b$ is $44$.

**Answer: 44**

lehigh-2022-30.title: Construction and bound
lehigh-2022-30.body:
Construction: split the students ranked $1$ to $36$ into consecutive blocks $L_1,\dots,L_8$ of sizes $1,2,\dots,8$ (in increasing rank), and the students ranked $37$ to $64$ into blocks $U_1,\dots,U_7$ of sizes $7,6,\dots,1$ (also in increasing rank); let club $j$ be $L_j\cup U_j$ ($U_8=\varnothing$), which has $8$ students. Club $i$ wins $8(8-i)+i(i-1)$ matches against club $i-1$: this is $56,50,46,44,44,46,50,56$ for $i=1,\dots,8$, so $K=44$ is achievable. (One can verify the counts directly.) Bound: in each club look at its $4$th best student, and take the club $X$ whose $4$th-best student is the weakest of these eight. Club $X$ competes (as club $i$) against club $i-1$, whose top $4$ students are all better than $X$'s $4$th best. The $5$ students of $X$ ranked at or below its $4$th best each lose to those $4$ students: at least $20$ losses of the $64$ matches, so club $X$ wins at most $44$. Hence $K\le44$.

**Answer: 44**
